lesson.title: Build a Better ls CLI in Rust with Clap
lesson.goal: build a command-line tool in Rust with cargo that parses arguments

sources.title: Build a Better ls CLI in Rust with Clap

steps.title: Create project and parse path argument
steps.instructions: Run `cargo new best_ls`, add clap with the derive feature to Cargo.toml, and define `#[derive(Parser)] struct Cli { path: Option<PathBuf> }` parsed with `Cli::parse()` in main. Run `cargo run -- -h` to see the generated help.

targets.caption: Add clap with the derive feature
Derive Parser for the Cli struct

explanations.topic: clap's derive feature makes argument parsing easy
Option<PathBuf> as the first positional argument
Parser derive adds the parse method
Using -- to pass args through cargo run
Reading the generated help: usage, arguments, options

hints: Add clap to [dependencies] in Cargo.toml, and make sure the "derive" feature is enabled.
Put #[derive(Parser)] above a struct with a single field: path: Option<PathBuf>.
Import it with use clap::Parser; and use std::path::PathBuf;, then call let cli = Cli::parse(); in main.
Run cargo run -- -h. The -- separates cargo's flags from your program's flags.
common_mistakes: Forgetting features = ["derive"], so #[derive(Parser)] can't be found.
Not importing clap::Parser, which causes a 'no function or associated item named parse' error.
Running cargo run -h without --, which shows cargo's help instead of your app's.
Using PathBuf without importing std::path::PathBuf.
Making path a required PathBuf instead of Option<PathBuf>, which changes the usage to <PATH>.

steps.title: Add version and about metadata
steps.instructions: Annotate the struct with `#[command(version, about, long_about = "best ls command ever")]`. Check `cargo run -- --version` and `cargo run -- -h`.

targets.caption: Version and about metadata above the struct
Clap now generates a version flag

explanations.topic: #[command(version)] pulls the version from Cargo.toml and adds -V/--version
Help output now includes the version flag
about and long_about set the description shown in help
Clap generates the CLI for you so you can focus on program logic

hints: Add an attribute line directly above your #[derive(Parser)] struct.
Use #[command(...)] with the keywords version and about.
Add long_about = "your description" inside the same #[command(...)].
Run cargo run -- --version, then cargo run -- -h, to see the result.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the -- in cargo run -- --version, so cargo prints its own version instead of your tool's.
Writing #[clap(...)] with clap v4 syntax mismatches, or misspelling long_about as longabout.
Forgetting the "derive" feature for clap in Cargo.toml, so the command attribute is not recognized.
Putting the #[command] attribute on main or a field instead of the struct.

steps.title: Validate path with colored errors
steps.instructions: Set `let path = cli.path.unwrap_or(PathBuf::from("."))` and use `if let Ok(does_exist) = fs::exists(&path)` to print "Path does not exist" (in red via owo-colors `.red()`) or "error reading directory". Run with a nonexistent path to see the red message.

targets.caption: Check whether the given path exists
Red error for a missing path

explanations.topic: cli.path is an Option; unwrap_or defaults to the current directory "."
fs::exists returns a Result<bool>; if let Ok unpacks it
owo-colors crate adds .red() for colored terminal output
cargo build puts the executable in target/debug

hints: cli.path is an Option<PathBuf>. Use unwrap_or with PathBuf::from(".") so it falls back to the current directory.
fs::exists(&path) returns a Result<bool>. Wrap it in `if let Ok(does_exist) = ...`, then branch on does_exist.
Add owo-colors to Cargo.toml (or run `cargo add owo-colors`). Import `owo_colors::OwoColorize`, then call .red() on the message string.
Run `cargo run -- doesnotexist`. The `--` separates cargo's own args from your program's args.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the `--` in `cargo run -- path`, so the argument goes to cargo instead of your program
Not importing `owo_colors::OwoColorize`, which gives a 'no method named red' error
Passing path by value to fs::exists and then using the moved path later
Not importing std::fs or std::path::PathBuf
Using a Rust version older than 1.81, where fs::exists isn't stable

steps.title: Write get_files to list names
steps.instructions: Create `fn get_files(path: &Path) -> Vec<String>` that iterates `fs::read_dir(path)` and pushes each `file_name().into_string().unwrap_or("unknown name".into())`. Loop over `get_files(&path)` in main and print each name.

targets.caption: cargo run lists the current directory

explanations.topic: Path::try_exists returns Err when existence can't be confirmed or denied
if let Ok(...) on fs::read_dir and on each DirEntry
file_name().into_string() returns a Result, so it uses unwrap_or with a default
No path argument defaults to the working directory

hints: Write a function that takes &Path and returns Vec<String>. Start with an empty vector and return it.
Use `if let Ok(read_dir) = fs::read_dir(path)`, then `for entry in read_dir` with `if let Ok(file) = entry`.
Push `file.file_name().into_string().unwrap_or("unknown name".into())`. In main, use `for file in get_files(&path) { println!("{}", file); }`.
common_mistakes: Forgetting `use std::fs;` or `use std::path::Path;`.
Passing `path` instead of `&path` when the function takes &Path.
Treating `into_string()` as an Option. It returns Result<String, OsString>, and `unwrap_or` still works.
Declaring the vector without `mut`, so `push` fails to compile.
Calling `.unwrap()` on `read_dir`, which panics on unreadable directories.

steps.title: Collect file metadata into FileEntry
steps.instructions: Define `struct FileEntry { name, e_type: EntryType, len_bytes: u64, modified: String }` and `enum EntryType { File, Dir }` with strum's `Display` derive, filling them via `fs::metadata(&file.path())` in a `map_data` function. Print the entries with `{:#?}` to verify sizes and types.

targets.caption: File or Dir, printable via Display
Debug output showing sizes and types

explanations.topic: Designing a FileEntry struct for metadata (name, size, modified)
Using an enum to represent file vs directory
strum's Display derive turns enum variants into strings
fs::metadata returns a Result, so match with if let Ok
Bug: passing the base path instead of the entry's path to metadata
Extracting the logic into a map_data function

hints: Add a struct with name, an entry-type field, a u64 size, and a String modified field, plus a two-variant enum.
Add strum (with the derive feature) to Cargo.toml and put #[derive(Debug, Display)] on the enum; FileEntry needs #[derive(Debug)] to print with {:#?}.
Inside the read_dir loop, use `if let Ok(meta) = fs::metadata(&file.path())`, then pick EntryType::Dir when meta.is_dir() else File, and use meta.len() for the size.
If every entry shows the same type and size, you passed the directory path to fs::metadata instead of file.path().
common_mistakes: Calling fs::metadata on the directory path argument instead of each entry's file.path(), so all entries report the same metadata.
Naming the field `type`, which is a reserved keyword in Rust (hence `e_type`).
Forgetting #[derive(Debug)] on FileEntry or EntryType, causing a `doesn't implement Debug` compile error with {:#?}.
Adding strum without the derive feature (strum = { version = ..., features = ["derive"] }), so `Display` can't be derived.
Treating fs::metadata as returning Option (if let Some) instead of Result (if let Ok).

steps.title: Render a styled colored table
steps.instructions: Add tabled, derive `Tabled` on FileEntry, build `Table::new(get_files(&path))`, apply `.with(Style::rounded())` and `.modify(Columns::first(), Color::FG_BRIGHT_CYAN)` etc. for columns and the first row, and rename headers with `#[tabled(rename = "Type")]`, `"Name"`, `"Size B"`.

targets.caption: Renamed headers appear in the table

explanations.topic: What the tabled crate does: print structs as ASCII tables
Choosing a table Style (rounded)
Targeting columns/rows with modify to add colors
Renaming headers with #[tabled(rename = ...)]

hints: Add tabled to Cargo.toml (cargo add tabled) and add Tabled to FileEntry's derive list.
Replace the print loop with `let table = Table::new(get_files(&path));` and `println!("{}", table);`.

Make the table mutable, then call `table.with(Style::rounded())` and `table.modify(Columns::first(), Color::FG_BRIGHT_CYAN)`; use `Columns::one(n)` for other columns and `Rows::first()` for the header row.
Put `#[tabled(rename = "Name")]` above a field to change its header text.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to derive Tabled on FileEntry (and on the nested EntryType enum, which also needs Display), causing trait-bound errors.
Not declaring the table as `let mut table`, so `.with`/`.modify` fail to compile.
Importing the wrong Style/Color (e.g. from owo-colors/colored instead of tabled::settings).
Using an out-of-range column index in Columns::one, so the color never shows.
Putting the rename attribute as #[tabled(name = ...)] instead of #[tabled(rename = ...)].

steps.title: Format modified dates with chrono
steps.instructions: In map_data use `if let Ok(modi) = meta.modified()` and convert with `let date: DateTime<Utc> = modi.into(); date.format("%a %b %e %Y").to_string()`, else an empty string. Run `cargo run -- src` to see the Modified column.

explanations.topic: Why add the chrono crate for dates and times
meta.modified() returns a Result<SystemTime>
Converting SystemTime into DateTime<Utc> with .into()
strftime-style format specifiers for printing dates

hints: Add chrono to Cargo.toml (e.g. `cargo add chrono`) and import `chrono::{DateTime, Utc}`.
In map_data, replace the modified field with `if let Ok(modi) = meta.modified() { ... } else { String::new() }`.
Inside the if, write `let date: DateTime<Utc> = modi.into();` and return the formatted string from `date.format("%a %b %e %Y")`.
Run `cargo run -- src` and check the Modified column shows dates like `Tue Mar 4 2025`.
common_mistakes: Naming the binding `mod`, which is a Rust keyword. Use `modi` or similar.
Forgetting the `DateTime<Utc>` type annotation, so `.into()` can't infer the target type.
Not adding chrono to Cargo.toml or missing the `use chrono::{DateTime, Utc};` import.
Returning `date.format(...)` without `.to_string()` or `format!`, which causes a type mismatch with the String field.
Leaving out the else branch, so the if-let expression has no value when modified() fails.

steps.title: Add --json output flag
steps.instructions: Add `#[arg(short, long)] json: bool` to Cli, extract `print_table`, and when `cli.json` print `serde_json::to_string(&get_files(&path)).unwrap_or("cannot parse json".to_string())` after deriving `Serialize` on FileEntry and EntryType. Run `cargo run -- -j` and `cargo run -- --json`.

explanations.topic: Clap #[arg(short, long)] creates -j and --json from a bool field
Extracting the table output into print_table
serde with derive plus serde_json for serializing to JSON
Serialize must be derived on the nested EntryType enum too
unwrap_or fallback string when serialization fails

hints: Add a `json: bool` field to your Cli struct, then run `cargo run -- --help` to see whether it shows up.
A plain field becomes a positional argument. Annotate it with `#[arg(short, long)]` so it becomes a -j/--json flag.
Add `serde` (with the "derive" feature) and `serde_json` to Cargo.toml. Put `#[derive(Serialize)]` on both FileEntry and EntryType.
In main: `if cli.json { println!("{}", serde_json::to_string(&get_files(&path)).unwrap_or("cannot parse json".to_string())); } else { print_table(path); }`
common_mistakes: Omitting #[arg(short, long)], so json is treated as a required positional argument instead of a flag
Deriving Serialize on FileEntry but not on EntryType, which causes a 'Serialize is not implemented' compile error
Adding serde without features = ["derive"], so #[derive(Serialize)] is not found
Forgetting `use serde::Serialize;`
Running `cargo run -j` instead of `cargo run -- -j`, which passes the flag to cargo rather than to the program
Using println!(serde_json::to_string(...)) without a "{}" format string
